raw_response:
I've been working this land for 30 years. I know what my soil does and what my family needs. My husband and one of my sons work off-farm now, so I need crops I can mostly manage myself, with them helping during the busy times — wheat harvest and cotton picking.

My 8.2 mu splits naturally. I put 5 mu into wheat-maize rotation, the way it's always been done around here. The other 3.2 mu I keep in cotton because cotton money is better, even though it wears me out. I can't afford to give up cotton while my grandchildren are still young and expenses are high.

For wheat, I plant in October the same improved variety I've been buying for years — it's reliable. I put down phosphate fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea twice. I irrigate four times: before sowing to get a good seedbed, at jointing, at heading, and once more at filling. I spray herbicide in winter and something for rust or aphids before harvest. My neighbor told me rotary tillage after maize is enough and saves fuel, so I do that.

After wheat I go straight to maize in June. I buy hybrid seed, everybody does now, yields are too different not to. Maize is easier — I broadcast fertilizer, irrigate when it looks dry, and spray twice. No-tillage works fine here, the straw breaks down.

Cotton is the hardest. I plough in spring, transplant seedlings in late April. I irrigate five times, and I spray every two or three weeks through summer because bollworm and aphids never let up. It's tiring but I've done it so long I know the rhythm.
